scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Trance of the Ghatusari
This is Ghatu dance. 16th century.
on_screen: Title card: Ghatu dance · Nepal · 16th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is believed to have originated in the 16th century in the Lamjung district of Nepal, following the death of a local Gurung king.
Research suggests the tradition emerged during a period of Hindu influence in the region.

While the Gurung people follow a blend of Buddhist, Bon, and local Hindu customs, the Ghatu dance incorporates elements of Sati, which are considered alien to traditional Gurung culture, suggesting a synthesis of local and incoming cultural practices.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance commemorates the tragic story of King Pashramu and Queen Yambawati.
It is performed during the Baisakhi Purnima festival.
The Sati Ghatu is performed from Shree Panchami to Baisakh Purnima, while the Bahramase Ghatu can be performed throughout the year, though it is generally avoided until Shree Panchami.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by two main dancers, the Ghatusari, who represent the King and Queen.
The dancers enter a trance state and perform with meticulously slow, deliberate steps.
The performance is divided into segments called Dandi.
Watch for Trance state.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Two main dancers (Ghatusari) perform the roles of the King and Queen.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music consists of songs sung by men, passed down orally through generations.
The primary instrument is the Madal drum.
Listen for the Madal drum.
The music is characterized by male vocalists singing in an Indo-Aryan language, accompanied by the percussive, rhythmic beat of the Madal drum.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear traditional Gurung cultural dress and jewelry.
A signature element is a crown crafted from flowers and roasted paddy.
Props are handmade each year for the performance, including representations of a horse, a comb, and a bow and arrow.

scenes.title: The people
narration: King Pashramu and Queen Yambawati are the central historical figures depicted in the dance.
The dance is primarily associated with the Gurung community of Lamjung but is also performed by the Magar, Dura, Balami, and Kumal communities.
The tradition is handed down orally from generation to generation.
